utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Good afternoon, Madam Registrar. Could you kindly call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you so much. We've got everyone here except Mr. Bourgon. Mr. McCloskey is absent as per agreement from yesterday. Mr. Thayer has taken over. And when we adjourned yesterday, it was Mr. Zivanovic who was in possession of the floor. There was one notebook which was not available that Mr. Zivanovic wished the witness to have a look at. I don't have an identification number for this notebook. Perhaps you can state that and Mr. Thayer can confirm whether this is available or not. It wasn't available yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Before the beginning of our session today, I checked and the notebook is now available and it has indeed been brought into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It hasn't been brought into the courtroom? Why is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, it has been brought into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thought I heard it hasn't. But I heard you -- anyway, so perhaps we can land it over to the witness. Witness, good afternoon to you and welcome back.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will make every effort to finish your cross-examination today.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Just for the record, Mr. President, this notebook is marked with the ERN 0080-4523 on the cover page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Thayer. Witness, have a look at that notebook, go through it, please, and let us know whether you're familiar with it. In the meantime, you can sit down, Mr. Zivanovic, and give him time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Could we have in the transcript, the witness is sifting through the notebook in the meantime, please. Yes, I notice General Gvero.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED GVERO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Your microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED GVERO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Again, I do not have e-court and I don't have the transcript on my screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It will be attended to immediately, General. You may sit down. In the meantime I am sure your colleague General Pandurevic will accommodate you and we'll look into that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED GVERO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The others, you don't have any problems with your monitors? Okay. Thank you. Yes, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have leafed through the notebook carefully, and save for the handwritings that could be similar, I have not found any other elements showing that this could be a notebook from my unit, and I will refrain from mentioning the name of the unit because you all know the unit's name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In fact, don't, because we are in open session. We can go into private session if Mr. Zivanovic wishes to pursue this matter further.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please go into private session? Because I would like to put a few more questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, certainly, Mr. Zivanovic. Let's please go to private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For the record, Mr. Zivanovic, for accused Popovic has finished his cross-examination. We've reverted to open session. Mr. Ostojic for Colonel Beara will be commencing his.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would prefer to stand if it's all the same to you and you don't mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No it's just to make you feel more comfortable to be able to switch off the microphone because I think your assistant now will have a -- quite a job.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm sure he's very capable, Your Honours, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm sure, too. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you are addressing me, then good afternoon to you, too, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And I was. Sir, I'm going to cover a little bit about your background and certification you received. You told us yesterday and the day before that you received both a C and B category certification for amateur radio, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you distinguish for me what the difference is between a C category amateur radio operator and a B category amateur radio operator, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The difference between the category C, first difference, would be that category C is a club category, whereas category B could be a private sign, and in essence it differs in terms of content and subject matter to be mastered for passing the exam which means a certain speed for telegraphic signs for a higher number of prefixes, which means names, abbreviated names for countries. Then a higher number of acronyms that ham radio operators use to communicate, and a significant knowledge about electronics. This refers to category B, which requires for one to be knowledgeable about electronics.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And what about category A? How do you distinguish category A from B, sir? Basically the same way, that category A is the more experienced, more knowledgeable amateur radio operator, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: An amateur of A category, first of all, differs from the rest in the constraints applicable. B category operator is constrained in terms of the strength of antenna radiation in certain volumes that operators of A category may use as opposed to those of category B.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, do you possess any professional certifications or diplomas involving surveillance operations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the term surveillance, as I heard it in my interpretation, in my headset, I know that I passed a course for commander of visual and observation stations. If this is what you are referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, close. Do you know if there exists any professional certifications or diplomas for operators in the field of intelligence or surveillance?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar, sir, with whether or not the JNA at the time that you were in the JNA and subsequent to that, had a specialised school for intercept training?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: During my national service in the JNA, I did not learn about that, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: How about after? Did you ever come to learn that, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Immediately prior to the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What was that called, sir, that one-year specialised training?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, sir. I don't know the title.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If we may have Exhibit P-02297 up? It's under seal but if we can just not have it broadcast and I think I could ask him questions and we should be able to follow it rather --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for that, Mr. Ostojic. Let's see it and we are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: As long as it's not broadcast I could just identify it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, before us you have Exhibit P-400297. It's a list of individuals, if you could identify using only the number of on the left-hand side of the name of those individuals, starting with number 2, which individuals had a certification as an amateur radio operator and then tell us, if you will, also, what that certification was.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Person under 3 had a certificate but I cannot really recall either C or D. Then the second-next name --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay, let's redact -- let's see if it shows up in the transcript in any case, but we still have to redact. It's not -- the name mentioned by the witness is not in the transcript but he did mention it so transmission broadcast of the proceedings of that part needs to be blocked, referring to -- starting page 18, line 23, until here. Until here. I mean, I want to play it safe.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Maybe I can do it a different way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He sticks in the numbers without mentioning names.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I wanted to shorten it but I will go through the numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Number 2, sir, do you know if he had a certificate as an amateur radio operator, just yes or no?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: How about number 3? Did number 3 have a certificate as an amateur radio operator?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What certificate did he have, to the best of your recollection, what category?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just said I don't know which category.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And do you know if he had a category that was higher than yours, a B category?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That did -- was not so, sir. I'm certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know, sir, if the person identified in number 3 had the same category as you, that would be the B category?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, I did not know which category certificate he had.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. How about number 4, sir? Was he certified as an amateur radio operator?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: How about number 5, sir, was he certified as an amateur radio operator?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And what category certification did number 5 have?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At least a C.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: All right. The next one, number 6?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Same, at least a C, category C.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: How about number 7?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure about number 7 but I think he had no certificate.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And number 8, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Number 8, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: How about number 9, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You don't need to go through all the numbers until number 12. The rest, apart from number 12, for whom I'm not certain, did not have any certificates.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm sure I understood you sir so 9, 10 and 11 did not have any certificates as an amateur radio operator and for number 12, you're uncertain, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. May I add that I'm not sure about person number 10, whether that person had a certificate.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. I understand now. Thank you. Sir, did you ever give a statement or were you ever interviewed by the Dutch authorities?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And on how many occasions, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: On several occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you help narrow it down between let's say the numbers 10 to 100?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's below ten.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know if that was in connection with the report that we from time to time used here as being called by the acronym NIOD, NIOD?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, but I'm not familiar with this acronym.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That's fair. Maybe I'll try to remember what it is. I think I had the Netherlands institute of war documentation but they have abbreviated it from what I could see as NIOD. If you're not familiar, sir, you can just tell us that and we'll move on.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I was contacted by persons from that institute -- from this institution.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know looking at the exhibit that we have in front of us, P-02297, what other individuals, 1 through 12, also gave statements to the representatives of the Dutch authorities?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I don't know whether you will be happy with my answer, if I tell you only about the persons that I'm sure of. And I am not excluding any others. Is that going to satisfy you as an answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It's very easy to delight me. So that will be sufficient. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm certain about some, and I don't know anything about others. There are some that I'm not certain about. I'm not sure about person under 11. I believe so but I can't be sure of that, if that can be of any assistance to you. Person number 6, person number 5, I know that they were contacted by Dutch authorities and the same goes for person number 3. I'm not sure about number 4, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Anyone else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of the persons listed here, including person number 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We'll get back to that NIOD report a little later. Let's talk about the equipment that you had at the mountain top, if I could refer to that. I think we have in the past in open session. Sir, are you familiar with a piece of equipment called an RUP-12?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what that is?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. It's a radio set. It's a receiver, and the frequencies are 30 to 70 megahertz. It has three switches for choosing channels, and the lowest channel leap is about 50 kilowatts and the power is about two kilowatts but not always. It depends on what channels it works. The battery is below the radio set. In a nutshell, it is a military radio set, a radio receiver and transmitter.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me, sir, given the descriptions that you've given us about the megahertz, the kilowatts, et cetera, that this is a sophisticated piece of equipment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, given the conditions under which this device can operate, and given its advantages in that respect, I would say yes. However, when it comes to its design, I would say that it is rather obsolete.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And, sir, am I correct that you're familiar with the RUP-12 because you, in fact, had used that sometime prior to 1994, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And, sir, will you agree with me that your unit did not have this RUP-12 in 1995 at all, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must say that I'm confused. You -- your question is, "Your unit did not have," so am I supposed to say yes or no? Let me explain, then. My unit did not have that device in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me, sir, why you think that RUP-12 is an obsolete type of military equipment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Given the range of devices that followed RUP-12, one can say that the latter is rather obsolete. However, it does have its advantages, one of them being that it can operate under all sorts of conditions, even the most extraordinary ones, based on the characteristics that it features, its durability and reliability t could still be a usable device. However, when contrasted to some other devices that are currently on the market, I'd say that it is rather obsolete, very obsolete.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That confirms the suspicion I had in the back of my mind, that when he said in the first place that it is a rather obsolete piece of equipment, whether he refers to the present or to --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I was going to go to that. Thank you for reminding me of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I was tempted to put the question before.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: At any time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So it's obsolete today but we are talking about 1995. Was it obsolete in 1995 as well, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. It was. Let me just give you an example to illustrate this. If you take a so-called Motorola, this is so much more practical and it has so much of the features that make it more usable.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, as you yourself say, some of the advantages or features of the RUP-12 is that it helps reduce distortion, interruption, in conversations that you might be intercepting, does it not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It does, sir. However --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Please continue. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Propagation on this type of waves can be the cause for somebody to -- who wants to listen into that station at a distance, to be disrupted by signals that come from even a further distance. Still, when this device is listened to within the prescribed range, or even a bit further than that, within certain limitations, the RUP can be recorded in three steps on the analyser.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, what was the receiver that you were utilising in your unit on that mountain top in July of 1995, if not the RUP-12? It was a military unit first and then, if not, what type of receiver were you using?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're asking about my platoon and the receiver RUP-19, as far as I know we didn't use that. You also asked me which receiver it was. We had several radio amateur receivers, the AR-3.000, ICR-100, ICR-7.000, ICR-7100, and for a while, ICR 9.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And can you tell us --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't want to interrupt my learned colleague, unless I have to. I just noticed that answer at line 19 to 20 is unclear, at least to me, as from the transcript. He's referring to a unit in answer to question, what did you use, but then it says, "as far as I know we didn't use that." And there can be some clarification of the record, I just don't know whether that's a translation issue or perhaps I'm misunderstanding but it appears unclear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are 100 per cent right. Mr. Ostojic, I leave it in your hands, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, there seems to be some confusion in the record and it's probably my fault but can you just tell us what RUP machine you used on your mountain top with your unit and which receivers you used?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, in our platoon we only used receivers. I don't know whether I should proceed or do you want to say something.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Just so the record is clear, just list out the receivers. I think you had already, but just so the record is clear, and I think we have them, just list out those receivers or only those receivers that you used in your unit on that mountain top in July of 1995.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, of course. I've already done it, and I shall repeat it. We used AR-3.000, which was a radio amateur device, an ICR-100, an ICR-7.000, an ICR-7100 and for a while we also used an ICR-9.000. But not at that time, so you can omit that. We had used the last one before that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Sir - just before the break, I think we are break being at quarter of - you testified in the Blagojevic case, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, the Blagojevic case, on pages 3847, line 3, and also on lines 8 through 9, you make the following statement and this is in connection with what Your Honour asked you the other day regarding telephone communications. I'm just trying to have a better understanding because I didn't quite understand your answer. You state there, "There was a rupture in our communication." And then you -- further down on lines 8 through 9 you state, "We were facing lots of practical and technical problems." Now, sir, with respect to that, my question is: What time period was there a rupture in your communications?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me, this doesn't jog my memory at all. I don't know what this refers to. This is just a short quote from the whole thing, so I can't be of any assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. How about the fact that you were facing lots of practical and technical problems? Do you recall when that was, sir? When were you facing lots of practical and technical problems?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that at the beginning, when we first arrived as this facility, we experienced problems, one of them was getting to the mountain itself. I remember that. I also remember that we had our problems with water supply. We received water from some pumps from a valley that had to pump water into our reserve up on the mountain, and the whole setup caused a lot of problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And what year was that, sir? What years did that cover?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm talking about the winter of 1993 and 1994. This is when those problems were very much pronounced. Also, we had electricity outages, and I even think that there were some restrictions that there were some planned outages of electricity. This was done on purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, you spent sometime talking about cryptographic equipment. Do you know what that equipment is?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You mean the make? Or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just generally, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Shall we deal with that after the break?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: At your pleasure, Your Honour, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think because if it's a whole description of the function of the equipment, I think it will take a couple of minutes. So let's have a -- we need a -- 30 minutes now because of that -- 30-minute break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Nikolic would like to address the Trial Chamber. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just briefly, Your Honours. Regarding the issue that was raised about the Prosecutor's submission regarding Rule 92 ter, the Defence for Mr. Nikolic does not have any objections to the qualification of the witness. However, we would like to point to certain circumstances that we have noticed in the submission, and after that, I would like to announce a period of seven days which we require in order to be able to respond to that submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. We had prior information of that and you will be granted those seven days, and I suggest that the rest of the others that haven't come back to us try to tie up with you, Madam Nikolic, so that if you have a common front on this it would be better. Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, yesterday you inquired of the tentative dates that we may have planned to those two witnesses --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, the 7th and the 10th.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: The 7th and the 11th respectively, Your Honour, I think that gives us enough time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, the normal period of time would lapse on the 7th so we had in mind of advancing it in any case, but Madam Nikolic indicated the 28th. More or less we can extend that to the 1st, even to the 1st, so that's not a problem. The important thing is that we have some kind of advance notice on what the situation or what your position is so that we can act accordingly.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So, I can bring in the witness? Yes, Eva, please. What happened to the temporary co-counsel that was appointed to replace Mr. Bourgon during his absence?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will explain, Your Honours. He was appointed just in case I cannot be in the courtroom. He follows from his office and in case that I'm not able to attend sessions, he acts as a stand-by and replaces me in order to avoid any delays.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Thank you. Because there were rumours that he decided to walk it all the way from -- but so that's not the case. All right. Thank you. And I suppose, Madam Fauveau, that Mr. Petrusic is functioning in his role as co-counsel now? Or not yet?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I haven't yet received the decision from the Registry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. But you are aware of our decision, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. Thank you very much for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Ostojic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And go --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I was informed, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You have all the time you require to finish your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Much appreciated, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, sir, before the break we were starting to discuss cryptographic equipment. Just generally if you could describe what cryptographic equipment is?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Cryptographic equipment consists of a device that protects information, be it verbal or digital information, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, is it your testimony, sir, that your unit on that mountain top in July of 1995 actually had cryptographic equipment at the facilities?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll tell you what we had. We had a computer, as our means for communication, which was connected to the network modem, and protection was performed by using certain codes or keys. Those were used on the computer and that's how we protected information. There was a certain code consisting either of figures or letters that had to be typed in and that was used to pack the contents of the text that were shipped towards a different user.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. I don't fully understand your answer and forgive me for that. Can you identify the type of equipment by name or initials that you utilised on that mountain top in July of 1995 that would fulfil the description of a cryptographic piece of equipment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I've told you what I know, and I've listed the equipment that we had. Now, as to the way this was done, I've already told you I'm not best suited to talk about that. You should ask the person who was in charge of that, the cryptographer, the person who was added to our unit from the platoon PEB unit. This person shared everything with us and did everything for us but by formation he belonged to the unit that was part of our unit and I'm sure of -- I've made myself clear now.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And what is that person's name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether you want me to really give you his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I really do.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, I don't know whether we are in private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't know that it may be an issue but we'll go into private session if that's a concern if that's okay with the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: That was just my --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That's fair, thank you, Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just a couple more questions, Mr. Witness, in connection with the equipment. The search for frequencies that the personnel, including yourself, at the mountain top in July of 1995 was conducted always manually, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The frequency scanning could the done the way you describe it or it could also be done by automatic search of frequency or scanning, for which there was a programme and we could scan one part of the area that we found interesting and the device was capable of searching those frequencies on its own. It would stop at certain frequencies that would appear as a shift visible on the scale and it would also stop at certain periods, as required by us. It could stop for a longer time, it could skip the certain frequency, or it could stay on it for five seconds, for example. This is what our machinery could do.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: But forgive me nor asking, in the pictures that we saw of the UHER and of the receiver with the other components, I didn't notice an automatic directional searching mechanism on that machine. Are you telling us that the machines that you utilised actually had an automatic directional searching function?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Every ICOM device belonging to that period had that possibility, and did what I have just described. Would you set up a programme in a programme for zero to nine, which means ten given programmes. You decide on the frequency area and the frequency shift, together with the type of modulation that that device would search. And it is only then that it starts operating either manually or automatically depending on what we wanted to do at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, do you remember, sir, if this automatic directional search function actually stopped when it reached a frequency or did you have to depress a button so that it could continue to scan for frequencies?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, this depended on the requirement of the person who searched the area. Any of the three ways could be utilised. Likewise, there is a difference between the search of the RRU-1 area. This is like doing things manually, by any other radio set, although this equipment had a -- much better functions. However, when it came to RRU-800, this could not be done automatically. As for the quality and for information, one had to do it manually based on previous information on frequencies and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you for that. If we can now talk about the analysis and processing and reporting of the function of your unit in July of 1995, sir, can you first tell me what an analyst is?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: An analyst is a person who uses certain documents and knowledge in order to form a picture of a person, a group or a formation, and all this based on the given elements, so that person draws conclusions based on those elements.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And you'll agree with me, will you not, sir, that in part, an analyst would try to figure some things out, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And yesterday, actually, my learned colleague who is celebrating Thanksgiving, he asked you to help him on page 14, line 20 to figure out certain meanings of an intercept that you took down on July 14, 1995, correct? I think he used the word "figure out." Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is there a problem or what?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Maybe he didn't understand the question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know. He has to tell us.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I thought you were asking me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is there a problem with you answering this question, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The interpreter apologised to me and said that he is having a problem because he doesn't know which word exactly I used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Then you can repeat that word. Okay, let's simplify it. You can repeat that word and the interpreters, I'm sure, will be as helpful as they have always been. So Mr. Ostojic asked you --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you can.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'll shorten it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, I'm not sure that you used the word. My learned friend Mr. McCloskey at the OTP used the word when he was discussing the intercept with you yesterday, specifically page 14, line 20, I believe, and he used the word "figure out," and we kind of agreed that figuring things out is what an analyst does and I just wanted you to recall that. And do you agree with me that that's the discussion you had in trying to figure out a certain intercept dated the 14th of July 1995? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I remember that, and the word that you used if it referred to the area scanning, I don't know whether the best word would be an analyst. Maybe it would be, partly, in its elementary form. However, when we use the word analyst, we thought of them as very capable people who worked down there at the command and who really performed miracles with the material that they had on their hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And sir, is it true and correct that you are not an analyst?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is true, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And sir, is it also true and correct that in fact no one at the mountain top in July of 1995, from the list that we have previously seen, no one there was even remotely considered to be an analyst, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is absolutely correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, let's talk about the processing of certain information. Is it -- am I correct that there was no real-time intelligence that was being processed at your unit in July of 1995? First let me ask you, do you know what real-time intelligence is?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sir, I would appreciate your explanation of the term.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'll be happy to share it with you. Sir, is it first your testimony that you don't know what real-time data is?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic, there may be -- I'm not saying that there is but there may be a -- would be a problem with interpretation of these terms. I would suggest that you explain to him the -- both terms and then you ask him whether he is familiar with that concept.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, real-tame data or real-time intelligence is information that is processed from one unit to another on a spontaneous or immediate basis, meaning at the time that it was being recorded, at the time that it was being taken down, that that material is transmitted directly to a superior or to another unit that it was reporting to. Real-time meaning, at the exact time or close to that time.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Respective of the fact that this has been a -- this term may be all encompassing, I do believe that I understand what this means. It means to send information as quickly as possible to somebody who is more capable of processing such data or information. Is that what you meant?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Close. But not as quickly as possible but in real time. At the exact time, spontaneous, when it was occurred. And if you're not familiar with it, we can move on, sir.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We could not relay information in real time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: In fact, sir, are you aware that the Dutch authorities in their NIOD report referred to your processing system at your unit as being crude?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that, sir, about this term.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, let's talk about the processing of this information and I'll try to, just in a nutshell, do it. When you heard the -- when you had the frequency set at a certain conversation that you were anticipating to intercept, you would write it down on a scratch sheet of paper and then the next step would be, from that scratch sheet of paper you would enter into a logbook that we've seen the last day or so, and then from the logbook, sir, you would then give it to the computer technician, if I can call him that, or the computer person, and that computer person would then type in the information from the logbook. And then from the computer, you would - what - print it out and then forward it, depending on whether it was a daily report or a priority or urgent report? Is that basically the process, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well let's talk about reporting now. When you have a report that says priority or urgent, who makes that decision that it's a priority or urgent report given the fact that you acknowledge no one including yourself was an analyst who analysed the intercepts that you were receiving?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me, sir, any of the operators could make this assessment. By the same token, the person could differentiate from what we had, and in terms of what the command would tell us about the type of conversation or the description of that state to us a certain conversation. Which means that we did not have any significant problems in this respect. If we did have, it was only in the beginning, where there were some objections, criticism. But this does not -- is not valid for the period that you are asking me about.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, we'll stick to the period I'm asking you about, July of 1995. Can you tell us, sir, if you had a courier always available at your facility just in case there was a priority or urgent message that needed to be run over or carried over to your command?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, we did not appoint a person who would be a courier unless there were special circumstances when a courier would be appointed, but when it was business as usual, we would not appoint a courier. If we had a need for one, then this would be done by the person for whom it would be easiest to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, do you know on July 14, 1995, who was the couriers that you used?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Trust me, I could not remember that, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Since we are talking about reporting, I'm a little confused on another issue that I'm sure you can help me with. When you have a daily report, is that a report that is being sent to the command on a daily basis?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I've discussed this already, and -- but I can always repeat, and further explain it. In a period where there would be no combat activities, where -- when we would not be required to report as quickly as possible and when we did not have any time sensitive information or intelligence, regular reports would be sent in the evening between 7.00 and 10.00 p.m., sometimes even later but in principle there was so.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I mean we saw the daily reports which I understood to mean once a day. Are you telling us that the daily reports on July 14th were sent out more than once a day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it, in the heading daily report, that was always put on top of the page. I'm not sure whether it was put on each. Even when we had several reports in a day, we would use this daily report heading. This means that we may have been mistaken in using that heading.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Is another reasonable explanation perhaps that above the line where it actually has the words, "daily report," that that was at least according to you someone that was coded or locked out because of some security reason?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I have not understood your question but I'll -- I can understand that part which I understood and which I presume you're asking me about. You mean only the heading was coded? Is that what you're trying to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know exactly what was coded but could you at any time above the line on the computer printout be able to change anything that was above the line in those reports that you sent out, including the title, which is apparently on some, if not all, the reports which says, "daily report"? Were you able to alter or modify that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I explained everything I knew about that already, and the cryptographer may be the right person to try to explain that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Fair enough. Sir, let me talk about another topic, it's called, generally speaking, chain of custody. And you mentioned a little bit about that the other day when you said that the log books that you kept were actually retained in a safe. Do you remember that general conversation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, when, sir, did you give your logbooks, specifically I think we are talking about logbook 9 involving the July 1995 intercepted conversations that you purport to have taken, when did you turn those over to the command?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot really tell you from the top of my head, believe me.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I do. Did the command ever give you a receipt or any documentation verifying the date in which you turned these logbooks over to them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. But during your asking of this question, I sorted out my thoughts about else I could tell you about the previous conversation. If command would not require that certain material would be delivered or -- then during a certain shift that material would be handed over or turned over during the subsequent shift.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So as you sit here, sir, do you know when in particular the logbook which is identified as logbook 9, when that was turned over to your command?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. But I can presume when it was supposed to be turned over.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. When?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was supposed to be turned over during the subsequent shift.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And, sir, do you know an individual by the name of Sveko Tihic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard the name in my headset. No. It's not known to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So you wouldn't know what rank, if any, he had, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't know, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Who, sir, at the command would you give your logbooks at the end of the shift that we were just previously discussing, to whom?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment before you answer that question, if by answering that question he would identify the posting, then we'll need to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We can just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do I need to repeat the question, Your Honour? I will, I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Once we are in open session, I would suggest you do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, based on the experience that you have, please explain what the significance if any is of making changes, modifications, alterations or additions to logbooks.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. At any rate, each modification, alteration, addition, may impact the credibility of such a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: But don't you agree with me, sir, that it would not only impact it, it could dilute the potential reliability of such a document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that in this respect, the question is pretty -- of such a nature, this is a very unspecific question. I'm trying to answer it, though. It could happen, sir, on a case-by-case basis. I wouldn't dwell into that -- delve into that but it would depend on the case in hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And we are just generally talking here about those --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But because of the generality of the question, and the kind of information you're trying to seek from him, I mean, Mr. Ostojic, come on.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We will get to it Your Honour, but I have one last question on this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: But generally speaking, sir, wouldn't you agree with me depending on the length of a text and depending on the number of changes, modifications, additions or alteration that is someone would make, it can, in fact, destroy the reliability of such a logbook or entry, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, had you stated in your question, if it pertained to just one text, but if it pertains to a whole notebook or logbook, I wouldn't dare answer such a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That's fair. I was relating and I misspoke. I wanted to say document and I said logbook. No, we are talking about one document, sir, and as you put it, just one text.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let's put it this way: My question -- my opinion about what you're asking me about is as follows: The meaning of a certain part of a certain document could be altered in the way that you hint at, which in my opinion depends on which part of the text is the salient and the important part, and there are people who make such assessments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Enough, enough. I think let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We are, Your Honour, thank you. I mentioned that it was the last question on that so thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, do you know the extension or telephone number of your boss or superior at your headquarters in 1995?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The question of whether he knows it? You're not asking him to tell us the number because if you are --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Of course, no, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you, are then we need to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: No. I don't need the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you, sir, in July --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: May I restate the question, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Witness for your patience. Sir, in July of 1995, when you were on that mountain top with your unit, did you know the extension or telephone number of your boss or superior?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me, I cannot tell you now if there is such an information in my documents, make use of it by all means, please, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Maybe I stated the question awkwardly. Did you, in July of 1995, know your supervisor or your superior or your boss's telephone extension or number?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. You probably mean his desk where he worked and not his personal telephone number at home. I used to know his telephone number at the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. And every one of those 12 or so people in your unit in July of 1995, they also knew the number of the superior or boss at the headquarters, did they not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't dare to go into such level of detail but I believe that sufficient number knew that the person, the cryptographer, had this telephone number and he knew it. I can only presume that a squad leaders knew the telephone number. I couldn't dare to say that the other personnel knew the telephone number.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, we were talking about figuring out certain items that you wrote down in this intercept that was transcribed. There was one in particular. Did you have a -- how did you decode the word "upper house"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, my interpretation was upper house. I believe that it was -- used the taller house in that conversation. I understood that word by its literal meaning, that that meant his superior, but in respect to those whom I had to forward the material to, that was the upper house.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. We'll get to that in few minutes, I hope. Let me ask you this, because you spent time the other day on page 36, lines 10 through 12, actually on Tuesday, discussing when my learned friend was asking you questions about being familiar with voices from the Main Staff, again page 36, lines 10 through 12. Sir, do you have any experience or training in voice identification?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: My training was in radio work, an and this was spent on ham radios, and this is what I had in terms of training. However, I believe that I owe to my good hearing that I can actually recognise voices.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: All right. So other than your good hearing, you have that experience or training in voice identification, correct, nothing else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: How about voice recognition? Do you have any experience or training in voice recognition?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I want to read, if I may, to you, sir, from page 36, lines 10 through 12 of Tuesday's transcript and I want to talk about there for a little bit. It starts, "When someone introduces himself to you ten or a hundred times, you should be able to tell that that's that person the next time. They don't need to introduce themselves." With respect to that question or with respect to that answer, sir, my question is: Why such a big range, ten to a hundred times? When were you, sir, able, after how many times to recognise a voice?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not always the same, sir. First of all, there were typical features of one's voice that imposed themselves and made you remember that person. And the -- second of all, the typical characteristics of the transmission was another feature that identified somebody's voice. And those two sets of characteristics were the ones that helped us recognise and identify certain people's voices.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, as you sit here today, having reviewed your logbook in preparation for your testimony this week, having testified in the Krstic case, having testified in the Blagojevic-Jokic case, can you tell us, how many times did you purportedly hear the voice of Mr. Beara?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to tell you that, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know, sir, that it was more or less than ten?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me, I don't know. Really I don't know how many times.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know, sir, in looking at your logbook number 9 that no where prior to the purported July 14th 1995 entry was Mr. Beara mentioned, referenced or identified as a participant in an alleged conversation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: In July of 1995, sir, did you even know what division, corps, or section of the army Mr. Beara was in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me put it this way: It's very difficult for me to say that as I sit here today. I don't know whether I knew it at the time or not. However, there must have been somebody who could have put me in the picture in that respect, but I wasn't really very much interested in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. We'll come back to that in a few minutes. Sir, let me show you Exhibit P-02312, which is for identification the packet of materials that my learned colleagues gave us yesterday, that we spent some time on yesterday. And once that is up, I'll ask the question. Sir, you have the first page, I believe, of that document, and, in that page, in glancing through it, I see that there were 11 out of 15 daily reports drafted on purportedly the 14th of July 1995. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You said one of the 15 daily reports dated the 14th of July 1995?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: No?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: They missed the other one but I'll try it again. Sir, of these 15 daily reports that I've counted and my learned friends can count them, of those 15, 11 are marked as being daily reports. Did you know that? So 11, not one but 11 out of 15 are marked simply daily reports on the top centre above the line of this exhibit P02312. Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you say so, I'm willing to believe you. There is no need for me to check that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, if we look at the next page of this document, with the Court's permission and the assistance of the usher, the next page I think has ERN number 0320-5316, the third page, sorry. That's the second of these reports. We are not going to go through all of them but I do wants to focus our attention on that and my learned friend yesterday mentioned the words below the line on the right-hand side, which is written in English, "Very urgent." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, this report, at least from my understanding of your testimony, this report, because it's marked very urgent would have been sent out immediately and it wouldn't be considered a "daily report," am I correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And am I also correct, sir that the "very urgent" is below the line because of these keys or codes or locks that you had that the analyst wasn't able to put the words "very urgent" anywhere above the line, correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Simply, Your Honour, because we have had discussion about the word analyst, I don't know if that was an intentional use. It's been translated as analyst, that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I thought that was only restricted to certain aerial images but I didn't know what were why the analyst couldn't -- fair enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I'm simply referring to the discussion that pertained to the technical role of somebody you described as an analyst which I believe his testimony clarified, that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I understand now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You can deal with that because --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I understand now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: At the moment, I couldn't really take down your reaction. And I think it was pretty obvious, but -- so, let's go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, am I correct that the "very urgent" is below the line because of these keys, locks or codes that you earlier testified to and that the surveillance operator wasn't able to put the words "very urgent" anywhere above the line, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I would not wish to discuss the technique that the cryptographer used and I would not offer any assumptions as to what they could or could not change. I've already told you what I know about that. However, it seems to me that the different thing is at stake. This material this CSB, SDB Tuzla, that is the addressee, and it was sent very urgently. Whether this was sent through our connection, through our unit, I wouldn't know. I could not draw that conclusion based on this material. I don't know whether this material ended with us or whether it was forwarded. I don't know what the requirements and agreements were. In any case, the person could have sent it this way. When the body of the text starts, one of my assumption, which could be explained by the person who actually did it, would be that the body of the text was not on the floppy disk or the text above the line was not on the floppy disk. I don't know how they exchanged their materials. I'm sure that the person who actually did it could be of more assistance with that regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now if we could turn to the 15th daily report of the 14th of July 1995, which has ERN number 0320-5339, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think we need to go into private session with respect to some of these documents given, if they are going to be scrolled to a certain point there may be some identifying information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I take your word for it. Let's -- do you disagree with that, Mr. Ostojic, or no?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, I always prefer to be in open session. I wouldn't scroll to the name but -- whatever, that's fine. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Or else, unless we agree not to broadcast the -- visually the documents. All right? Then we can remain in open sessions, with the understanding also, Witness, that while we are taking all these precautions, you need to do the same thing and you must not mention any names directly. If you need to, then tell us and we'll go into private session. Yes. We have document number 15, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: May I proceed, Your Honour? Yes? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, we have document number 15 in front of us on the e-court. Here, if you can see that the word "PRIORITET" is actually typed in above the line and in the other instance we discussed, the word "very urgent" was typed below the line. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you just one more time explain to me how these keys and locks worked with items that you previously testified to that were above the line that were purportedly locked out and were unable to have any access by anyone in your unit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer? You're getting fed up, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, we have had the line of questioning on a number of occasions and the answers have been consistent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There question has been asked and re-asked, and we've had constant uniform responses to it. Just -- again, we are still in an indulgent mood. One more time and that will be it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That's fine. I don't agree with my learned colleague that they're consistent but I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, if you look at the initials or the abbreviation, I should say, below the line, "UCC ...". Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. And that is an abbreviation for the word "participant" in B/C/S, is it not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, we know so that from your prior testimony that the word "priority" was added by someone else in your logbook and we also know from your testimony, sir, that the other participants that were added, namely "X" and "Y" were added by someone else; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the X in the heading, I'm not sure. The colour is somewhat indistinct. There is black and blue at the same time, but you're right about the Y.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And nowhere in the section that was consistently prepared by your unit and its members under participants, nowhere in this 0320-5399 no where does it mention or reference Mr. Beara as being a participant in the conversation, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, we've seen that you made, in my opinion, forgive me for saying this, several, if not many, changes, additions, alterations and modifications to this logbook entry. Why didn't you just simply add, as you have made with other alterations, the name Beara right after the name Y?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please scroll up just a little bit? I would like to see the relevant portion. I believe that I have already answered that question several times. I've already explained how this BE was added. At first it was B, and then e was added. It had been listened a number of times and when this all ended, it turned out to be the way you see it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, and that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You haven't answered the question. The question is: Mr. Ostojic is referring you to that first -- or actually it's the second line, where, strictly speaking, you are defining the subject matter of the intercept, and there, you have Major Jokic stated, put down. You have Badem put down. Someone else put also X and Y. The question is, why didn't you also insert the name Beara on that line? That is the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me put it this way: All the while I had a switch board operator under Badem, every time, and after that, another person would join the conversation whom I could not hear, and then when the switch operator called that person, judging by the course of the conversation led by Jokic, in my book, from then on, this was Beara.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We'll talk about your book in a few minutes, sir, and how you came to that conclusion. But right now I want to know, since you went through the trouble of correcting the actual line which designates who the participants are and another person in your unit apparently added other participants in the -- on that line, why didn't you, sir, at that time, when you were adding the name Jokic or identifying the duty officer from Palma or correcting it from being Palma to Palme, why didn't you just simply add the name Beara on the top line where it clearly lists in every document the participants in certain conversations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're right, sir. I have should have done that. I should have added him as well. However, just like you said it yourself, "epsilon" and "priority" were added by another person, and I suppose that this was done in haste. This is the only reason I can propose. And finally, when the text was edited, it was sent as soon as possible to reach the other party as quickly as possible. And this is the only explanation I can offer.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, isn't it reasonable that given what you claim to be your experience and certifications and given the multiple intercepts that you yourself took down and transcribed with your unit, that in fact in no other area in the logbook do you omit to list the actual list of participants, if you believe that they were actually participants in an intercepted conversation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the title I also believe that this was a mistake. Well-spotted, I should say.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, in preparing for your testimony here and in your prior two testimonies that you've given in the ICTY and your interviews before the Dutch authorities, sir, did you ever find an intercept that you wrote down that had in excess of 15 changes, modifications, additions or alterations except this one, on the 14th of July 1995, involving Mr. Beara?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If my answer can help you, if I put it this way, I would say that I don't think so. I don't think I ever have.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And I looked at some of those logbooks, sir, and I don't find that there were any even remotely close to the number of changes, modifications, alterations that you made in any other entry others than this one of the 14th of July 1995 which you purport to involve Mr. Beara. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, because of the translation that I received, I would kindly ask you to repeat the question and I'll try to focus on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'll try to shorten it as well, sir. Can you identify for us, sir, if any other intercepts of yours had changes, modifications, alterations, or additions like the one that we are discussing now, namely the intercept involving, purportedly, Mr. Beara?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, if you exclude part of your assertion from your question, then I could answer. It's very difficult for me to answer your compound questions. If you could break it down in two then I could take each of the portions of your question at a time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're going to oblige.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, when I say "change" I'm referring to, like, for example, the change that you highlighted for us from a small D to a capital D in one of the entries. On this entry that we are talking about, we are only talking about this entry. When I say modification we are talking about the name Beara where you went with a black pen and then you stated, I believe, that you, in the second letter of the word, clarified that it was an E. Alterations, sir, we are talking about the circle that you made with the black ink and the dot that you made with the black ink next to the word "hello." For addition, sir, we are talking about the word "priority" which was an addition to the text. We are talking about the word or letters X and Y. We are talking about the additions, sir, of the letter E after the capital letter B on no less than eight occasions. Sir, can you tell us if any others intercept that you have ever reviewed, given your two prior testimonies, your preparation in this case, your interviews with the Dutch authorities, have you ever seen, of yourself, any such purported intercept with so many changes, modifications, alterations or additions like this one?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so, sir. There were texts, however, which involved a lot of noise, and I know that in such conversations there might have been a lot of corrections, but not as many as we saw yesterday. For example, letter B was altered on five or six occasions and the rest of the things that you've mentioned in your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And I think with all due respect to you, sir, there were probably another three to five, what I could find, changes or alterations in your intercept that the -- my learned colleague didn't cover with you because they were simply in a different part of the conversation, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, is it true that you were unable to hear the person you claim was Mr. Beara at the beginning of the purported conversation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. I gave my previous answer in a haste. I rushed into it and I did not complete my answer. If you don't mind, I would like to complete my previous answer but also answer the question that you have just put to me. Yes, I know that there were such differences that you have just referred to. I'm aware of that and I agree with you. However, when it comes to whether I heard Beara or allegedly heard him, the document speaks for itself. I adhere by what I wrote down, and as to what I did not write down, what I omitted to write down, I'm really sorry about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let's look at the conversation because we happen to have it conveniently in front of us, sir, and isn't it a fact that you were indeed unable to hear the person you claim was Mr. Beara at the beginning of the purported conversation? You couldn't hear him, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, it's very difficult to determine. I believe that this was at stake for the most part but we can also assume that there were some ambiguities that he murmured or there was some other reason. It's not easy just based on the dots that -- to say that I couldn't hear him. I might have heard him but I might not have understood him. Whatever the reason, none of them can be confirmed with certainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Witness, quite candidly, if you did hear him at the time, don't you think that you would have written down what it is that he said on your logbook?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He's just explained that, Mr. Ostojic. He's just explained that. "I might have heard him but I might not have understood him. Whatever the reason none of them condition confirmed with certainty," so I think he's given you his answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you it was my understanding that when you put three or several dots flex to a participant in a conversation, that that meant you could not hear them and therefore you could not write down what the contents of their conversation was. Now, is it your testimony, sir, that it was perhaps that you couldn't understand him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I say, sir, on the basis of those dots, I cannot really say what was the right reason for them being there. So that I wasn't certain or something that certainly wasn't usable wouldn't be put down, and this is why three dots would be put in that place because that information would have been lost or unutilisable.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. And, sir, is it fair to say, looking at this logbook and this transcript, that it was not usable or it was lost, that you weren't able to hear that person you claim to be Mr. Beara on six separate occasions? Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So does that help us maybe have a better understanding if you were simply unable to hear him or you just couldn't understand him purportedly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, since we've clarified this once, I do not believe that there is a need for us to dwell on it further. Either of these, if they are in the text, that means that they stand in for something that is unusable.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And do you, sir, as a non-analyst, as a surveillance operator, do you make that decision that words by someone are unusable?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know, sir, that there were six of us on that facility at that moment. It doesn't matter but there was more people than one single person. And if all of us had tried and said, "No use, it cannot be done," then only then would we give up.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, let's go down to the bottom where you made one change but without -- it's not being broadcast so we are okay. Down at the bottom, sir, where you have the word, well, this might be difficult because it's not typed out properly. How about if we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session. Let's make it simple, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, and I would ask that we have the original logbook put on the -- placed on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I have full trust in your caution.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
