utterances.text: Sir, we are going to place on the e-court now 2D39, which was the document we previously looked at, which was your purported intercept entry of 14 July 1995. So if we could have that back on? No. Those are his notes on the UHER.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, one moment, one moment, one moment. Let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: The transcript does show that it was IC 000440 but really I need IC 00040. Which was yesterday used, I believe, on the first page of that document. If we could just scroll down so we could have the full ...

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, we are looking here at the -- there exhibit, IC 00040 and my question to you, sir, on that page, it's obvious that you were not introduced or Mr. Beara purportedly did not introduce himself at any time at this point, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. He did not introduce himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, I understood your testimony, from page 56, line 18, Tuesday, to be that if a participant doesn't introduce himself in a conversation, that you would write the letter X next to the conversation that you would hear. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, if you exclude the possibility that somebody else may introduce that person in the conversation, then you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I don't know if I understand your answer. Who would have introduced him other than himself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I believe that I've already covered that ground, but doesn't matter, I can reiterate. When we come to a certain part of the text where Mr. Jokic is in conversation with other persons, and then suddenly he agrees to a conversation and we see who sought him, then this is it, this is how we know how it happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if we can look at the next document, which is page 2, IC 00041, which also can be in open because I think the third page is the one that cannot, this is the second page of your log?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. You have now used "your" --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: The log.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, "Your log." This is what we have. I don't know if this is being transmitted, this page.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is it? Why not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What I'm worried about is that if Mr. Ostojic says, "your," automatically now anyone would know that this is this guy's handwriting and there will and few people who might recognise it. That's my concern. All right. I am assured that this document has not been broadcast, but was it broadcast yesterday when he was marking on it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. I think we can safely proceed, but try to avoid --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I will, I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, we are looking at this second page, and within that page, sir, am I correct that six out of the eight entries that you have, that's placed in there under "Be," after you had modified it, that there is no words that you could hear or sufficiently enough capture, as you put it, to be able to write down?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. For us to be able to use it, yes, exactly how you say it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And on Tuesday, my learned friend asked you, on page 54, line 23, how important accuracy was in taking down purported intercept conversations and I think your answer was, very important. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And would you agree with me, sir, that the notations that you make are also important, such as when you make dots or put a comma, a period, or a question mark or symbols like that? That's also not only important but very important?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. That is very important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Before I forget, things being what they are now, even though this document was not broadcast, I want to make sure that it is, when tendered, it is kept under seal, because the number has been mentioned by you, so it needs to be under seal, even though it's not signed. It only has his pseudonym. It needs to remain under seal. And likewise, I think the two -- the other two, the one that preceded it and the one that followed it. All right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It should be under seal. Thank you. Sorry for that interruption but we have responsibility that we need to attend to.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, the interests of time, sir, let's take a look at the two out of eight portions of a conversation that you purport and claim that it is of Mr. Beara. Do you see that, sir, there is two separate occasions that you supposedly record what that person that you claim is Mr. Beara said in response to Major Jokic, do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I can see that at the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And just so we are on the same page, there are seven words total in that -- those two sections, correct? If we can perhaps have the usher scroll up and we could focus on the bottom, I don't believe it's on that page, any identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is if you recall yesterday we had got to there, we couldn't move any further down, and we had the same document brought up clean and he marked number 16, and we had a question, a whole argument what was the last number on the previous one so we need to go to the next one.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: No, no, no if we could just zoom in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's not there.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, part of it is, I think. We will take it one at a time if it's okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: This is one part, sir, of the two parts of the eight conversations that you purport or claim belong to Mr. Beara. Do you see that, on the bottom of the page it starts with "Be," then a dash, and then the text. Do he see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I can see six words and two punctuation marks.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Perfect. That's what I see as well. Sir, the first set of words, we will take them three at a time if you don't mind. The first set of words it says, "Why number 155," do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, at that point, do you think, because accuracy is so important, that a question mark should have been placed after that "why number 155" instead of a comma?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, since we see that the sentence is composed of two questions, as far as I know about orthography, I placed the question mark at the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. I think in the English version, by the CLSS, they actually put a question mark right there but that's not of your concern. Let me ask you this, sir: In understanding or interpreting this, "why number 155," is it -- am I correct, sir, that the person you claim to be Mr. Beara doesn't know why or is uncertain as to why he should be calling extension 155? Would that be accurate?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: While I was listening to the conversation, this is how I understood it. Had I understood it differently, I would have modified it, and I would have shown and demonstrated that I wasn't thinking that this is how it unfolded.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, sir, as you sit here, do you know whose extension 155 was at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe I knew at the time, sir, but I do not know now.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, let's look at the next three words, sir, where you purport that the conversation that was intercepted and claim that it was of Mr. Beara, he says right there, "Where is that?" Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the part of the text, "where is that," there is a question mark, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm not asking you that, sir. I'm asking you for the words as well. It's translated, "Where is that?" Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's stated so.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, is it clear from that that we can deduce that in, in fact, the participant that is speaking here has no idea whatsoever where extension 155 is, nor what extension 155 was, correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I think we've reached the limit of this witness's competency to answer that question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think so. How can he answer that question? You can argue that but he can't answer that question. You can argue the point later.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If I may proceed. I understand that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He will not answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If that's the Court's ruling, that's the court's ruling. If we can have 3D31 placed on the e-court, please. If I may this should not be broadcast because it does have the individual's identification on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think there is an understanding, the technical staff know exactly how we are proceeding so -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: As they are bringing up it I'll ask him.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, as you sit here today, you know whose extension 155 was in July of 1995, do you not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, do you remember that in May of 1995, the Office of the Prosecutor had you write in your own handwriting an intercept which contained the extension 155?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Judge Kwon just asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: May 1999. Thank you, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember this detail now.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: In this exhibit that we have in front of us, if we can turn to ERN number 00778135, maybe that will help refresh your recollection, sir. It's the same Exhibit number 3D31.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, that's your handwriting on this document that we see in front of us, 00778135 which is captioned "handwriting sample notebook blank" and below it is your handwriting below the typed text, is it not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And below it you actually are writing from a different intercept, some extension 155. Do you see it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There is also a secret code next to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. And the secret code which was broken is the word, "Panorama," correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And for our sake again, although I think we know it, Panorama was a secret -- purportedly a secret code word for what, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the Main Staff of the VRS army.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, do you reasonably think that Mr. Beara, who was chief of security in the Main Staff, that he would not know the extension of 155 and who it belongs to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Again, I mean you're asking -- I don't even need to hear your objection. You're asking the witness to explain for Mr. Beara. How can he? I mean, you can argue that point later, but you can't ask the witness to explain whether supposedly if this is Mr. Beara, who is speaking here, whether he was -- he knew or didn't know whether he was pretending not to know, there are so many possibilities. I mean, why ask the witness to give you that information?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, because, Your Honour, I think -- because, Your Honour, given what the Court said on Monday, to put my case to the witness, I am doing just that and because of the fact that it's not that someone may have said something but it was a mistake by the operators. Given some of the things that this witness has said and some of the other documentation that the Court will see, it's not only highly unlikely, Your Honour, but it's impossible that the person this individual thinks was Mr. Beara was in fact Mr. Beara because he would have known and he should have known that extension. And he recorded it as such. And now we are going full circle in light of the fact that this witness specifically said that there was distortion, couldn't hear six out of eight times. And it's not an argument that I wish to make at this time, but I would like to put to the witness that given all that, is it possible, likely and clear that he made a mistake and that that witness, that person that he claims was Mr. Beara, was in fact not Mr. Beara?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then, I have a confirmation that you've got it all wrong, Mr. Ostojic. The way to go about it then is very simple. You put to the witness that in your opinion, it's highly unlikely if not impossible that Mr. Beara in his capacity that you mentioned would not be privy to P155 and you ask him whether he would stand by his affirmation in these documents that it was Mr. Beara who was talking at the other end. But not the way you have put it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How can you expect him to tell you how clever or not clever or how informed or misinformed was Mr. Beara at the time, if it was Mr. Beara, who was at the other end of the line on that day? Because that stands to be proved in any case.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. I'll accept that question but before I put that question to the witness, may I ask him one other?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm not stopping you from putting questions that are legitimate ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, we know from not only while were you there in that mountain top in July of 1995 and in your meetings with the Prosecutor on May 11th, 1995 -- 1999, that the Panorama 155 extension belonged to an individual named Toso. We know that, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe you know that, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... your handwriting on the e-court which has "Panorama 155," dash, some word, another dash and then the name Toso. Do you see that? And the word that's in between is what?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Boss or head.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... after the word sef or boss, what is the name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Boss and then Toso.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, as the Court put it and I'll try to put it just as fairly to you, and I apologise in advance if I don't, if we presume or if I tell you that Toso was a person by the name of Tolimir and extension 155 was for the Main Staff, as you've indicated that panorama is the code word for Main Staff, and if I put to you, sir, that Mr. Beara was the chief of security in the Main Staff, wouldn't you agree with me, sir, that it's not only a possibility and not only a likelihood, but it's rather clear that the person that you claim you heard in this intercepted conversation on 14th July 1995, was not Mr. Beara?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would beg to differ, sir, with regard to the text, because I am not the one who can alter history.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, is it fair to say that a person who was chief of security of the Main Staff, that it's reasonable to infer that they would have known or should have known the extension 155 of the main headquarters and particularly of its superior?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You have come back to what I've told you please don't ask again of the witness. I mean, the witness cannot answer that. So next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, if we look at the last word that you have of this conversation, that you purport to have overheard from a person you claim to be Mr. Beara, it's one word, I would rather that we don't put it on the screen because it might capture the name, but the word is, and I think we could all see it, is the word "molim." Now, the Prosecutor on Tuesday suggested that when he read that the word molim means or is in interpreted as being "yes." Will you, sir, agree with me, and just for the court's record it's on page 19, line 18 of I believe yesterday's transcript, page 19, line 18, of yesterday's transcript, will you -- do you agree that the word molim can have different meanings depending on the context of a conversation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, you know very well that I had to write down what I heard. I was not in a position to interpret the meaning of the word. Maybe you should talk to one of my superiors about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Do you recommend I talk to the same two individuals you've identified before for us or is there someone else?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, because I think, if I understand you well, I mean, if I don't, please correct me, but if he's listening to this conversation and the word "molim" is used in his language, what he will put down is "molim." It's only when it is interpreted for our purposes that the question can arise whether it has been translated as it should or whether it has been given another colour or another interpretation which is not the right one.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: True.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So if that is the case, why ask him? Because he heard "molim," I would have put down "molim."

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: True, but there is another part of it, Your Honour, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, in a different context the word "molim" can actually be used with a question mark after it if you say something like "excuse me" because you didn't hear a question or "excuse me" because you didn't hear part of a conversation, isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. However, I am not to be the judge of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That's fair, sir, but given that the six words prior, that, as you claim, are attributed to Mr. Beara, have a question mark, since he questioned not only where but what or who, and then apparently Mr. Jokic says something else, and then the response is "excuse me," but there is no question mark, you being a man who said that accuracy is very important, would it have been inaccurate or wrong to put a question mark there and, if so, why didn't you, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I didn't put a question mark because when I heard that "molim," I heard it the way I transcribed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to just quickly because I know we are running out of time and I apologise to the Court and to my colleagues, and to you, sir, on November 4th, 2003, you were asked about the Dutch institute and the study that was done with respect to the intelligence in Bosnia or the Bosnian intelligence and this was the question on page 3873 of that November 4th, 2003, transcript. It states as follows: "And they are quoting from the Dutch institute here, line 12. "Taking the Bosnian efforts as a whole, it must be concluded that the service responsible for signals, that's" - you know what signals is - quote, "was simply too undermanned and poorly equipped to fulfil its mission adequately though there were many intercepts the processing, analysis and reporting were totally inadequate, intercepts were not typed out immediately in a word processing programme but transcribed by hand in a logbook. Tapes bearing messages were reused and hardly any use was made of computers to process and disseminate the data flow." Your answer, sir, was as follows, answer on page 3873, line 21, "Madam, I have to tell you that in view of the fact that you have read out a paragraph by, as you say, an eminent expert writer or whatever, who wrote about what was happening at the time, about a whole army. What I can say is that I partially agree with what you have read." You continue on: "But for me to know precisely what the conclusion of the book is, I would have to read the whole book, if you will allow me to say." Sir, I'm asking you with respect to the NIOD report which is the Dutch institute study that was done on the Bosnian intelligence that was read to you essentially some of their conclusions specifically of your unit and others, where they felt that it was inadequate, poorly manned, understaffed, poor equipment. Sir, you answer part of that question by saying that, "I partially agree with what you ever read." Can you tell me what parts you disagree with, sir and what parts you agree with the conclusions made of NIOD of your intelligence given the fact that you and many others were interviewed by them?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think I will -- do you think you can answer this question in the next five minutes? Or will you still require the whole text of the NIOD report to be made available to you to read to answer the question, the compound question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If I may Your Honour I'm only focusing on the parts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's a perfectly legitimate question but I want to know whether we can bring it to a conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We can, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You have also thought a lot of other things today and you were wrong. So, Mr. Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The gentleman has noted very well that I agreed with one part of that statement, i.e., that text that had been read out to me. I agree that we were poorly equipped, that there were -- there was a lot to be desired in terms of the machinery, such as receivers, antenna systems, scanning systems and so on and so forth. However, those things were more than satisfactory for the work that we did. And as for lacks that we felt, there it was a lack of tapes, recording devices. In that respect, I would agree when it comes to the equipment. Also, we had a lot of problems with the lack of a constant source of energy. That's why we had to use batteries and generators. We used generators all the time. And this all was an additional burden. If we had had good conditions, we would not have needed all that. I also agree that we were undermanned. We worked around the clock. People were exhausted. We did what we did and that's how things were. In view of our requirements I believe that we met the demands of those who had appointed us and they were satisfied with our work. That's why I'm saying that in that part of the context within the context of analysis and other estimates, I'm sure that you will have an opportunity to hear the person who will have more to say about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And just quickly if you can just on with the Court's permission flip -- to your right, the book on the first or the cover page, if you don't mind. The book that's to the right of you that's on the ELMO, if you can just please close that book for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Or maybe Madam Usher could help. Yes, and we could have that on the screen. That would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: On the screen not on the ELMO. He wants to see the cover page.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, we discussed briefly there the cover page and I know we are running out of time where it says do you see 29/II, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, is it your testimony that there should exist a book that has 29/I, since this is supposedly the second part of that book 9, number 29, correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He answered that yesterday. He said that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I didn't get -- I -- I didn't think it was quite clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, I've asked the Office of the Prosecutor to find and give me a book logbook 29/I, and they told me that they don't have it and don't know if it exists. Do you know what happened to that logbook 29/I?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, sir. I would like to help you, if I only could.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you. We stop here but before we adjourn, I wish Mr. Thayer and all the others that come from the US and are celebrating Thanksgiving day, a belated Thanksgiving day. Your partners and friends and family members still over there, across the pond, on the other side, are about to start enjoying the day. So enjoy the rest of it. Thank you. Tomorrow morning, we have other business in another case, and we won't be able to start the sitting before at least 10.00, but please be here at 10.00 because if we finish the other business before, we will start at 10.00. Otherwise we will start a little bit later but it won't be much later. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 24th day of November, 2006, at 10.00 a.m. 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.01 p.m.,
